section.title: The City of Our God
section.sectionRationale: Closing this Korahite triad of Zion psalms, Psalm 48 praises Jerusalem as the city of the great King, language Jesus Himself uses in Matthew 5:35, and which finds its final fulfillment in the heavenly Zion, Hebrews 12:22, and the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21.
section.thesis: Zion's God-given security, dramatically proven when enemy kings flee in terror before her, becomes cause to walk her ramparts and tell the next generation, pointing forward to the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the living God that all who are in Christ have already come to.
section.frameNote: Four movements: praise for the great city and its holy mountain, verses 1-3; the kings who assembled and fled in terror, verses 4-8; meditation on God's loving devotion within the temple, verses 9-11; and the call to walk Zion's ramparts and tell the next generation, verses 12-14.

units.label: Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised
units.note: praise for the great city and its holy mountain

verses.text: Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, His holy mountain.
Beautiful in loftiness, the joy of all the earth, like the peaks of {{tsapon|Zaphon}} is Mount Zion, the city of the great King.
God is in her citadels; He has shown Himself to be a fortress.

units.label: They saw and were astounded
units.note: the kings who assembled and fled in terror

verses.text: For behold, the kings assembled; they all advanced together.
They saw and were astounded; they fled in terror.
Trembling seized them there, anguish like a woman in labor.
With a wind from the east You wrecked the ships of Tarshish.
As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the LORD of Hosts, in the city of our God: God will establish her forever. Selah

units.label: Within Your temple, O God, we contemplate Your loving devotion
units.note: meditation on God's loving devotion within the temple

verses.text: Within Your temple, O God, we contemplate Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}.

Your name, O God, like Your praise, reaches to the ends of the earth; 
Your right hand is full of righteousness.

Mount Zion is glad, the daughters of Judah rejoice, 
on account of Your judgments.

units.label: This God is our God forever and ever
units.note: the call to walk Zion's ramparts and tell the next generation

verses.text: March around Zion, encircle her, count her towers,
consider her ramparts, tour her citadels, that you may tell the next generation.
For this God is our God forever and ever; He will be our guide even till death.

tsapon.gloss: Zaphon, the mythical mountain of the gods in Canaanite religion, believed to be the dwelling place of Baal. The psalmist provocatively claims this exalted image for Mount Zion instead, declaring the true God's mountain surpasses every rival claim.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion. Within the temple itself, the worshiping community's central meditation is not on the building's grandeur but on this quality of God's loyal, covenant love.

basic.context: This Zion psalm celebrates Jerusalem, God's holy mountain, as beautiful and secure, dramatically proven when a coalition of enemy kings saw the city, were struck with terror, and fled without a battle. Worshipers are called to walk its ramparts, count its towers, and tell the next generation of God's faithfulness.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's confidence rests not in Jerusalem's natural defenses but entirely in God's presence within her, so that the city's security becomes a living testimony, walked and counted and retold, of God's own faithfulness across generations.
basic.originalLanguages: Mount Zion is compared to the peaks of tsapon, Zaphon, the mythical mountain of the gods in Canaanite religion, provocatively claiming that grandeur for the true God's own mountain instead. Within the temple, worshipers meditate on God's chesed, His steadfast covenant loving devotion.
basic.typology: Mount Zion, the city of the great King, is the very title Jesus applies to God's throne in Matthew 5:35, while the psalm's confidence in an unshakeable, eternal city anticipates the heavenly Zion of Hebrews 12:22 and the new Jerusalem of Revelation 21, where God dwells with His people forever.
basic.christ: Jesus directly echoes this psalm's language when He calls Jerusalem 'the city of the great King,' Matthew 5:35, speaking with the very authority of Zion's true King, while the psalm's vision of an eternally established city finds its complete fulfillment in the heavenly Jerusalem believers have already come to in Christ, Hebrews 12:22-24.
basic.god: God is shown as the true defender of His city, present within her citadels, whose reputation and righteousness reach to the ends of the earth, and whose loving devotion is the very substance worshipers contemplate within His temple.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 5:34-35 has Jesus using this psalm's own title for Jerusalem, the city of the great King. Hebrews 12:22-24 declares that believers have already come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem. Revelation 21:2-3 pictures the new Jerusalem where God dwells with His people forever.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's celebration of Zion's God-given, unshakeable security, dramatically proven before fleeing kings, points forward to the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the great King that Jesus Himself names, and that all who are in Christ have already come to and will dwell in forever.

context.literary:
The psalm is built like a walk around a city. It begins with the name of the LORD and the mountain where He is praised, verses 1 to 3, then pictures the enemy kings approaching, seeing and running, verses 4 to 7. Verse 8 is the hinge: 'As we have heard, so we have seen.' The second half turns inward to the temple, verses 9 to 11, and then outward again to the ramparts, verses 12 to 14, with the closing command to tell the next generation. The psalm therefore moves from city to enemy, from enemy to temple, and from temple to wall, and it ends by placing the whole experience in the mouth of the children.

The narrative of the kings is told in staccato. 'They saw and were astounded; they fled in terror. Trembling seized them there.' The verbs pile up like men falling over each other, and there is no fighting in it at all. The story is cut so short that it is nearly comic: an army that arrives, looks and leaves. The great irony is that the kings assemble 'together,' verse 4, and yet flee in a panic that scatters them.

The verse that turns the psalm is 'As we have heard, so we have seen.' The hearing was through the fathers' stories, the seeing was the day of the deliverance. Faith in this psalm is not blind, since it is confirmed. And the psalm also begins and ends with the same claim, that this God is the God of the city: 'the city of our God' in verse 1, and 'this God is our God forever' in verse 14. The heart of the psalm is the meditation in verse 9, where the words shift from the city's walls to God's covenant love.

There is also a play on counting and telling. The Hebrew verb behind 'count her towers' in verse 12 is from the same root as the verb 'tell' in verse 13. What the worshiper numbers, the worshiper must recount.
context.historical:
The setting is Jerusalem in a time of siege or near-siege by a coalition of kings, and the most commonly proposed occasion is the deliverance from Sennacherib of Assyria in 701 BC, when an angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 men in one night and the king withdrew to Nineveh, 2 Kings 19:32-36. The psalm does not name the enemy, and the details fit but do not prove the identification. Other readers think of the coalition Jehoshaphat faced, 2 Chronicles 20. The psalm is best read as belonging to the memory of Jerusalem's deliverances.

The mountain of Zion was not high by the world's standards. The Hebrew of verse 2 compares it to Zaphon, a mountain on the north coast of Syria which Canaanite texts from Ugarit make the dwelling of Baal, the storm god. Zaphon's name also means 'north,' which is why some translations speak of Zion 'in the far north.' The footnote in the BSB notes that Zaphon was the most sacred mountain of the Canaanites. To a listener in Judah, hearing this was a bold claim. The mountain that Canaan gave to a false god is outclassed by a modest hill in Judah, because the great King lives there. The psalm takes over the language of a rival religion in order to say its own thing.

The ships of Tarshish, verse 7, were large trading vessels, and Isaiah and Ezekiel use them as a picture of proud commerce that the east wind shatters, Isaiah 23:1 and Ezekiel 27:26. The east wind is also the wind that drove back the sea at the exodus, Exodus 14:21. The footnote offers 'a fleet of trading ships' as an alternative, which underlines that the image stands for proud human power in general.

Finally, the walking of the walls in verses 12 and 13 fits the Israelite habit of making memory physical. Pilgrims came up to Jerusalem for the feasts, and to circle the city, count its towers and tour its citadels was to fix the story in the body. The 'daughters of Judah' in verse 11 are, as the footnote says, probably the villages around the city, who rejoice in God's judgments.
context.canonical:
Psalm 48 is the third of a run of songs about God's presence, kingdom and city, and it belongs with Psalms 76 and 87 in celebrating Zion. Psalm 76 describes the same kind of victory in the same kind of words, Psalms 76:3-6, and Psalm 87 sings that the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob, Psalms 87:2. Psalm 125:2 gives the picture of the mountains around Jerusalem as the LORD surrounding His people.

The prophets then complicate the song. They saw that people had heard it and misused it. Jeremiah warned against chanting 'This is the temple of the LORD' as though the building were a charm, Jeremiah 7:4. Micah said that Zion would be plowed like a field, Micah 3:12, and Jeremiah's defenders later recalled that this word had been spoken in the days of Hezekiah, Jeremiah 26:18. Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD rising from the city, Ezekiel 11:22-23, and Lamentations put the psalm's language into the mouths of mockers: 'Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?' Lamentations 2:15. That is a direct echo of Psalm 48:2, and it shows how the city looked when the defence was withdrawn.

The New Testament takes up the idea of the city on several levels. Jesus refers to Jerusalem as 'the city of the great King,' Matthew 5:35. He weeps over it and leaves its house desolate, Matthew 23:37-38. The writer to the Hebrews says believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22, and that here we do not have a lasting city, Hebrews 13:14. Paul speaks of the Jerusalem above, who is our mother, Galatians 4:26. And John sees the holy city coming down out of heaven, Revelation 21:2, 10-14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants his hearers to leave the temple with a memory in their legs. Most songs of praise ask you to feel something, but this one asks you to walk. It commands a tour: go round the city, count the towers, look at the walls. The purpose is given in verse 13, 'that you may tell the next generation.' Faith is meant to be handed on, and the way to hand it on is to have been there, to have seen, and to be able to say what God did.

The author also means to redirect confidence. The walls and citadels are real, and they are admired, but the psalm never credits them. When the kings come, no defender is named. The city is safe because 'God is in her citadels,' verse 3. What the towers are for is to point to the one who dwells in them. A hearer who admires the wall and forgets the LORD has missed the psalm.

The last thing the author intends is a claim about the future. 'God will establish her forever,' verse 8, and 'this God is our God forever and ever,' verse 14. The first hearers were meant to believe that the God who had delivered would be their guide 'even till death,' whatever came. The song therefore turns a past rescue into a present trust and a lifelong promise. It is written to steady people who know the story and will one day be tested by it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a deliverance and a city's security. It does not teach that Jerusalem, or any earthly city, is unconquerable. The prophets would soon show that the city could fall, and they explained why: the people trusted the place and not the God, Jeremiah 7:4, and Micah 3:12. To read verse 8 as an unconditional guarantee for a physical city in every age is to repeat the error the prophets condemned.

What the psalm prescribes is a habit of remembering and telling. Believers are to look carefully at what God has done, to think about His covenant love in the place where He is worshiped, and to pass it on to the next generation. It also prescribes trust in God's presence more than in defences, and that carries over without any change. The church has taken 'the city of the great King' to point to the people among whom God lives, and to the city that is to come, Hebrews 13:14. A modern congregation is not asked to walk a wall, but it is asked to count the works of God and to tell its children.

debates.question: Is the defeat of the assembled kings in verses 4-7 a specific historical deliverance or a generalized liturgical picture of God's protection of Zion?

views.label: The psalm recalls a specific historical deliverance, most plausibly the failed Assyrian siege under Sennacherib in Hezekiah's reign, 2 Kings 19
views.case: The precise details, kings assembling and advancing together, then fleeing in terror without a recorded battle, closely match the sudden, inexplicable withdrawal of Assyria's army described in 2 Kings 19:35-36.

views.label: The psalm is deliberately unspecific, a generalized liturgical celebration of God's defense of Zion usable for any threat, not tied to one particular battle
views.case: The psalm names no specific enemy or king, using generic language, 'the kings,' that would allow the community to sing it in response to any threat across generations, not only one historical crisis.

debates.bearing: Either way, the psalm functions the same pastorally, inviting God's people in any age of threat to walk Zion's ramparts and retell what God has done, whether recalling one great deliverance or God's pattern of faithful defense across many.

debates.question: Does verse 8, 'God will establish her forever,' promise that Jerusalem could never fall?

views.label: Yes, Zion is inviolable
views.case: Some in Israel understood the psalm as a guarantee: as long as God's temple stands there, the city is safe, and it seems many in Jeremiah's day believed this. Passages such as Psalm 46:5 and Psalm 132:13-14 speak of God choosing Zion as His resting place, and the deliverance from Assyria seemed to confirm it.

views.label: No, the promise depends on God and on faithfulness
views.case: The prophets treated the city's safety as bound to obedience and to God's own presence, not to the building. Jeremiah's temple sermon, Jeremiah 7:1-15, and Micah's word, Micah 3:12, warned that Zion could fall, and it did. The psalm itself puts the security in God, so that when He leaves, as Ezekiel saw, Ezekiel 11:22-23, the security goes with Him.

views.label: The promise is fulfilled in a greater city
views.case: The New Testament takes the forever of the psalm to point to a city that cannot be shaken. Believers come to the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22, and look for the city that is to come, Hebrews 13:14. The earthly city was a sign of the everlasting one.

debates.bearing: The three views agree that the psalm puts security in the presence of God rather than in walls. They differ in how the forever is fulfilled, and the New Testament's answer is the city God builds.

debates.question: What does 'He will be our guide even till death' mean in verse 14?

views.label: He guides us all our lives, right up to death
views.case: The plainest reading of the Hebrew is that God will lead His people until they die. It fits the psalm's theme of lasting trust across generations, and it keeps the promise practical: whatever the years bring, He is the one who leads.

views.label: He guides us beyond death
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that the phrase can be read as 'beyond death.' The Hebrew consonants can also be read as the word for youth, or as the musical term seen in the heading of Psalm 46, so the reading is uncertain. If 'beyond death' is right, verse 14 belongs with texts like Psalm 73:24 and Psalm 49:15, where God's guidance and receiving extend past the grave.

views.label: A musical direction attached to the psalm
views.case: Because the same letters can be read as the term in the heading of Psalm 46, some think the phrase may be a note to the choir that has been joined to the last sentence. This view is possible but leaves the verse without its climax.

debates.bearing: The first reading is safest and enough for the psalm's message. The second is possible and is in harmony with what Scripture teaches elsewhere about God's care beyond death, though the verse alone cannot bear the whole weight of the doctrine.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says the LORD is 'greatly to be praised,' from the verb halal, the root of 'hallelujah,' in a form meaning that He is worthy of praise, joined to the adverb me'od, exceedingly. The greatness and the praise are given the same emphasis. Verse 2 says Zion is 'beautiful in loftiness,' from a word for height or elevation, nof, and 'the joy of all the earth,' mesos kol ha'arets. The claim is not that Zion is the highest mountain, since in that country it is not, but that it is the most beautiful and gladdening. The prophets can later quote the phrase in reverse, with Lamentations 2:15 putting 'the joy of all the earth' into the mouths of those who mock a ruined city.

The comparison with Zaphon is in the phrase yarkete tsafon. The first word means the far side or recesses of something, which is why translators offer 'the far north' as an alternative. On either reading, the point is that the name of a mountain that was sacred to a rival religion is used as a comparison and then outdone. Verse 3 says God is in her citadels, and the word for citadels is armon, a fortified palace tower, while 'fortress,' misgav, is the same word used in the refrain of Psalm 46, which suggests the two psalms were sung as a pair.

The sequence of verbs in verses 4 to 6 is telling. The kings 'assembled,' from the verb ya'ad, to appoint or meet at a set place, and 'advanced,' from a verb meaning pass over or cross, so they marched purposefully. They 'saw,' and 'were astounded,' and 'were terrified' and 'fled in haste.' Each verb is short, and the last two are in the same form, so that the rout is over before the sentence is. The 'pain like a woman in labor,' verse 6, uses a noun for writhing pain that is used again for other terrors in the Old Testament. It is the image of a body seized by what cannot be resisted. The east wind of verse 7 is the qadim, the scorching wind of the desert, which Scripture uses as an instrument of God's judgement.

Verse 9 says 'we contemplate,' from a verb that is disputed. Translators render it as ponder, meditate, or think on, and it may be related to a root meaning to be still or to compare. The object is God's chesed, His loving devotion, a covenant word for the faithful, steady love with which He binds Himself to His people. The place of pondering is 'within Your temple,' literally in the midst of it. The chesed is not admired at a distance but where God dwells.

Verse 12's 'count' and verse 13's 'tell' are from the same root, saphar, which gives us the Hebrew word for a scribe and for a book. The worshiper is to be a counter and a teller. In verse 13 'consider her ramparts' is literally 'set your heart to her ramparts,' a phrase that means to give attention with the mind, not only the eyes. And 'guide' in verse 14 is from nahag, to lead, the verb of a guide who goes ahead of those who follow.

typology.type: Zion, the city of the great King, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: Zion was the hill where God chose to dwell and where David's line reigned. Jesus calls Jerusalem 'the city of the great King,' Matthew 5:35, and He is the great King in person, entering the city on a donkey to the cries of the crowd, Matthew 21:5-9. Hebrews says that believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22, and Paul names the Jerusalem above as our mother, Galatians 4:26. The escalation is that the city is no longer bounded by walls and towers but is the people of God gathered to Him. The type falls short because the earthly city was destroyed, while the city of the Lamb is built by God and does not fall.

typology.type: The kings who assemble and flee, verses 4 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The kings gather against the city and are undone by fear before a blow is struck. The pattern is repeated at the cross and beyond. The rulers of the earth take their stand against the LORD and His Anointed, Psalms 2:2, and Peter applies that to the Roman and Jewish rulers who gathered against Jesus, Acts 4:25-28. At the cross He disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, Colossians 2:15. The final gathering of the kings against the Lamb ends in their defeat, Revelation 19:19-21. The type is limited because the psalm's deliverance was for a single city, while the victory of Christ is for all who are in Him.

typology.type: God in the midst of her, verses 3 and 8
typology.fulfillment: God's presence in the citadels was the reason for the city's safety. The presence dwelt in the temple, and 'Within Your temple, O God, we contemplate Your loving devotion,' verse 9. The Gospel of John says the Word became flesh and 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Jesus spoke of His body as the temple, John 2:19-21. In the last vision there is no temple in the city because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The type falls short because the temple was a place one had to go to, while Christ is God's presence coming to us.

typology.type: The next generation told, verses 12 to 14
typology.fulfillment: Israel was commanded to tell children what God did, and the great pattern is the Passover, Exodus 12:26-27, and Deuteronomy 6:20-21. The church has the same charge, that the works of the LORD be told to the coming generation, Psalms 78:4. In Jesus' great commission, disciples are to teach all that He commanded, Matthew 28:19-20. The Lord's Supper is the church's walk around the walls: 'Do this in remembrance of Me,' Luke 22:19, which keeps the deliverance fresh in the body. The type falls short because the tour of Zion was to a place, while the church's telling is to the nations, and the deliverance recounted is the resurrection.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the title in verse 2, 'the city of the great King.' Jesus takes up that very phrase in the Sermon on the Mount, forbidding oaths by Jerusalem 'for it is the city of the great King,' Matthew 5:35. He is not quoting a slogan. He is saying something about whose city it is, and He says it as a teacher with authority over the Law. Later the King enters the city on a donkey, in the manner of Zechariah 9:9, to the shouts of the crowd, Matthew 21:5-9. The great King of Psalm 48 has come to Zion.

It leads to Christ by the theme of God among His people. The whole psalm rests on 'God is in her citadels,' verse 3, and 'Within Your temple, O God, we contemplate Your loving devotion,' verse 9. John writes that the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us, and we saw His glory, John 1:14. Jesus called His own body the temple, John 2:19-21. What Israel contemplated in the temple, the covenant love of God, is seen in Him. He is the meaning of the chesed the worshipers pondered.

It leads to Christ by the reversal of the psalm's terror. The kings who saw and fled feel the shock of a God they did not expect. In the New Testament the rulers gather against the Anointed, and the rulers of this age are exposed at the cross, Colossians 2:15. Yet the greatest irony is that the King who wins does so by being defeated, and the city He saves is not saved by keeping enemies out but by taking their judgement.

It leads to Christ by the city that cannot be shaken. 'God will establish her forever,' verse 8, meets Hebrews: 'you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22-24, and the mediator of the new covenant is there. In Revelation the city has no temple because the Lamb is its temple, and it has no need of sun because the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:22-23.

There is also Jesus' sorrow over the earthly city. He wept over Jerusalem, and said its house would be left desolate, Matthew 23:37-38, which shows that the psalm's security was never automatic. He is the one who stands where the psalm's God stands, and He grieves as a true King who will not be kept out of His own city.

A word of caution. The psalm does not itself point to a future Messiah by name, and its walls, towers and ships are not codes for Christ. The links here rest on Jesus' own use of the phrase 'the city of the great King' and on the New Testament's teaching that the presence of God, once in the temple, is now in the Son.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows about God is that He is worthy of praise in a particular place. He is 'great' and 'greatly to be praised in the city of our God,' verse 1. He is not an idea. His greatness is known where He has acted and where He has chosen to be. That is the doctrine of God's presence, and it is held with care, since the psalm never suggests that He is contained by the mountain. His name and praise reach 'to the ends of the earth,' verse 10.

He is a God who defends without visible effort. The scene of the kings is remarkable for what it does not include: no battle, no general, no hero. It is God's presence that does the work. The east wind that wrecks the ships of Tarshish is His instrument, verse 7. This does not mean that He is unconcerned with human agents in other places, since He often works through them. But here the psalm wants us to see that when God guards His people, He is enough.

He is a God of chesed. The verse at the centre of the psalm is not about power but about love: 'we contemplate Your loving devotion.' The God who scatters kings is the God who binds Himself to His people by covenant, and the psalm makes the two inseparable. The strength of verse 3 is put at the service of the steadfast love of verse 9. He is a fortress because He is faithful.

He is righteous and just. His right hand is 'full of righteousness,' verse 10, and Zion is glad 'on account of Your judgments,' verse 11. The word judgments here is not a threat to Zion but the verdicts by which God sets things right, delivering the oppressed and turning back the proud. The daughters of Judah rejoice over justice. For anyone who has waited for God to act, this is important: His judgments are good news to those who trust Him.

He is eternal and faithful across generations. 'This God is our God forever and ever,' verse 14, is a claim about time. The God who acted in the days of the fathers is the same today and will be the guide 'even till death.' The tension the psalm holds is between the particular and the universal. He is 'our God,' and His name reaches the ends of the earth. He is present on one hill, and He is Lord of all.

For worship, the psalm teaches the church to contemplate. Praise here is not only noise but attention: to stand in the place where God is honoured and think about His love. It also teaches the church to be storytellers. A congregation that has understood this psalm will make sure that its children hear, in plain words, what God has done.

crossReferences.note: The LORD promises that the king of Assyria will not enter the city or shoot an arrow into it, and that night the angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 men. It is the deliverance most often linked to the kings who saw and fled, and it shows a city saved without a siege ramp being used.

A companion Zion psalm in which God's tent is in Salem and His dwelling in Zion, and He shatters flaming arrows, shield and sword. It celebrates the same kind of rout, and reading it beside Psalm 48 shows how deeply the memory of deliverance shaped Israel's worship.

The LORD has founded His city on the holy mountains and loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. Glorious things are ascribed to the city of God. It adds to Psalm 48 the theme of divine love as the reason for Zion's glory.

The stream that gladdens the city, God in her midst, the nations raging and the refrain about the God of Jacob as a fortress. Psalm 48 picks up that scene and adds the walk round the walls, so the two are best read as a pair.

Passers-by clap in scorn and ask if this is the city called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth. The words come straight from the Zion songs, and they show how it felt when the protection promised in the psalm seemed to be gone.

The prophet warns the people not to trust in the deceptive chant 'This is the temple of the LORD.' It is a needed correction to a wrong use of psalms like this one, and it makes clear that God's presence, not a building, is the security.

Jesus forbids swearing by Jerusalem because it is the city of the great King. He uses the psalm's own phrase for the city and thereby places Himself as the authoritative interpreter of who the King is and what belongs to Him.

Believers have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. The writer says the everlasting city of the psalm is where Christians already belong.
Paul says the Jerusalem above is free and is our mother. It gives the city a maternal face: the secure city of the psalm is the community that bears and nurtures the children of promise.

John sees the holy city coming down out of heaven, shining with the glory of God, with walls, gates and foundations. The wall the psalm asked Israel to walk round and count is here recounted with twelve gates and twelve foundations, carrying the names of the tribes and the apostles.

The city has no temple because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, and the nations walk by its light. It shows the fulfilment of 'God is in her citadels': the presence is the entire city, and the gates are never shut.

When a child asks what the laws mean, the parent is to tell the story of the exodus. It is the pattern behind verse 13 of the psalm: faith is handed on by telling what God has done, and the rescue is always retold to the next generation.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers the question of where God can be found. In Eden He walked in the garden, Genesis 3:8, and after the exile eastward the human family lived at a distance from His presence. The tabernacle and then the temple brought God to dwell among His people, and Zion was the place where that dwelling became a city. Psalm 48 is the joyful side of that gift: the God who was lost to view is in her citadels.

It also answers the question of what stands against God's people. The Bible is full of kings who assemble: Pharaoh at the sea, the coalition of Canaanite kings, Assyria at the gates, and Babylon after it. The psalm's account of kings who saw and fled is one instance of a larger pattern in which the LORD saves without the sword. Each rescue, from Exodus 14 to 2 Kings 19, is a signpost that the greatest enemy is more than a man.

The story does not end with the psalm. The prophets tell us the city can fall, and it does, and the glory departs. The people who sang of the city forever go into exile, and their songs become laments, Lamentations 2:15. The forever of verse 8 seems to be broken, and the story has to look for something more.

Christ is that something. The great King enters the city and is put outside it, Hebrews 13:12, and by His death and resurrection He opens the way to a city that cannot be shaken. His people have already come to the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22, and they live now as pilgrims who tell the next generation what God has done.

The new creation is the psalm made whole. The holy city comes down from God, with its walls and gates and foundations, Revelation 21:10-14. There is no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple, and the nations walk by its light, Revelation 21:22-24. The gates are never shut, and nothing unclean enters. The guide who promised to lead 'even till death' finishes the journey and brings His people home to a city where He will be with them as their God, Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: Psalm 48
sermon.why: Carson expounds Psalm 48's celebration of Jerusalem as an image of God's kingship and protection, tracing the psalm's trajectory from the historical city to the New Jerusalem of Christian hope, directly serving this study's movement from the earthly Zion to its heavenly fulfillment.

quiz.q: How does verse 2 describe Mount Zion?

options.text: Beautiful in loftiness, the joy of all the earth, the city of the great King.
options.note: This description claims for Zion the very grandeur pagan religion attributed to the mythical mountain Zaphon.

options.text: A small, insignificant hill of no particular beauty.
options.note: The verse explicitly praises Zion's beauty and loftiness, not insignificance.

options.text: A location soon to be permanently abandoned.
options.note: The psalm celebrates God's eternal establishment of this city, not its abandonment.

options.text: A city known mainly for its marketplace.
options.note: The verse's focus is on the city's beauty and its identity as the city of the great King, not commerce.

quiz.q: What happened to the assembled kings, according to verses 4-6?

options.text: They saw the city, were astounded, and fled in terror.
options.note: The kings withdrew without any recorded battle, a dramatic proof of God's defense of the city.

options.text: They successfully conquered the city.
options.note: The text describes their terrified flight, not a successful conquest.

options.text: They negotiated a peace treaty with the city's defenders.
options.note: No negotiation is described; the kings simply fled in terror at what they saw.

options.text: They laid siege for many years before withdrawing.
options.note: The text describes a sudden, dramatic flight upon seeing the city, not a prolonged siege.

quiz.q: What are worshipers instructed to do in verses 12-13?

options.text: March around Zion, count her towers, consider her ramparts, and tell the next generation.
options.note: This active remembrance ensures God's faithfulness is retold and not forgotten by future generations.

options.text: Avoid the city entirely out of fear.
options.note: The instruction is to actively approach, walk around, and examine the city, not avoid it.

options.text: Tear down the city's towers as unnecessary.
options.note: The towers are to be counted and considered as testimony to God's protection, not destroyed.

options.text: Keep the knowledge of God's deliverance secret from others.
options.note: The explicit instruction is to tell the next generation, the opposite of secrecy.

quiz.q: What does verse 14 declare about God?

options.text: He is our God forever and ever, and will be our guide even to death.
options.note: This closing declaration grounds all the psalm's confidence in God's abiding, eternal relationship with His people.

options.text: He will abandon His people once the present crisis ends.
options.note: The verse declares the opposite, an everlasting relationship and guidance, not abandonment.

options.text: He is only concerned with the physical city's defenses.
options.note: The verse's scope is a personal, eternal relationship, our guide even to death, not merely physical defenses.

options.text: He will guide us only until we reach old age.
options.note: The text specifically says His guidance continues even to death, not stopping earlier.

quiz.q: Where does Jesus quote or echo this psalm's language about Jerusalem?

options.text: Matthew 5:35, calling Jerusalem the city of the great King.
options.note: Jesus applies this exact psalm's title for Jerusalem to Himself as the true King with authority over the city.

options.text: The parable of the prodigal son.
options.note: That parable does not reference Jerusalem or this psalm's language about the city of the great King.

options.text: The Sermon on the Mount's teaching on fasting.
options.note: The teaching on fasting is unrelated to this psalm's language about Jerusalem as the city of the great King.

options.text: The cleansing of the temple.
options.note: While that event occurs in Jerusalem, Jesus's direct quotation of this psalm's title occurs in the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5:35.

questions: This psalm praises Zion's beauty as the city of the great King even before describing any deliverance. How often do you praise God simply for who He is, before asking Him for anything?

The enemy kings fled in terror simply from seeing the city, without any battle being fought. Where in your own life have you seen God provide deliverance in ways you did not have to fight for yourself?

Worshipers are told to walk Zion's ramparts and count her towers so they can tell the next generation, verses 12-13. What specific evidence of God's faithfulness in your own life could you deliberately pass on to someone younger this week?

Jesus calls Jerusalem 'the city of the great King,' echoing this very psalm, Matthew 5:35. How does recognizing Christ's own authority over this psalm's language change how you read its confidence in God's protection?
The psalm closes with the declaration, 'this God is our God forever, He will be our guide even to death.' What would change in how you face uncertainty if you held onto this same confidence today?

translationNotes.note: Zaphon renders the Hebrew tsapon, the mythical mountain of the gods in Canaanite religion, here provocatively claimed for the true God's own mountain, Zion, rather than any pagan rival.
The ships of Tarshish were large seagoing trade vessels, a proverbial symbol of human wealth and power broken here before God's power, compare Isaiah 2:16.
Our guide even till death renders a phrase some ancient traditions read as our guide forever, but the sense in either case is God's abiding, unending guidance of His people.
